neutral_facts.value: The prosecution alleged that three individuals, who were police officers on patrol, fired at a scooter carrying the deceased, resulting in his death. The deceased was traveling with two witnesses on a separate scooter. The witnesses claimed that the police officers flashed a torch light at them, causing their scooter to skid, and then fired shots at them, which led to the deceased's death. The witnesses managed to escape and later reported the incident. The prosecution also relied on the presence of empty cartridges at the scene, which were matched to the rifles of the accused. However, the deceased's injuries were caused by a .12 bore weapon, which was not recovered from any of the accused. The trial court found the eyewitness accounts of the witnesses inconclusive and the testimony of one witness unreliable, leading to the acquittal of the accused. The High Court dismissed the appeal, noting that the prosecution failed to establish the identity of the accused as the perpetrators.

After investigation, CBI submitted a charge-sheet against the accused persons (the respondents herein) under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (in short, “I.P.C.”) After taking cognizance on the police report, the Court of First Additional Sessions Judge, Dehradun charged Anil Kumar, Shyam Bihari and Arshad Ali (the respondents herein) for committing offence punishable under Section 302 read with Section 32 I.P.C.
the application seeking leave to appeal under section 378 (3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (in short, “the Code”) was rejected and in consequence the Government Appeal was dismissed.
the High Court by the impugned order allowed the delay condonation application but rejected the application seeking leave to appeal and dismissed the appeal accordingly.
the appeal is dismissed.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the deceased was shot by persons wearing police uniforms, and the three accused were patrolling the area with rifles, and their presence at the scene was confirmed by eye-witnesses and evidence of cartridges fired from their service rifles. They also relied on the false cross version of the incident (Case Crime No.48A/87) to indicate police action leading to the deceased's death.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove that the accused were the ones who shot the deceased. The deceased died from a .12 bore gunshot, not a rifle bullet, and some cartridges found at the scene did not match the rifles of the accused. The eye-witnesses could not identify the accused, and the testimony of PW-15 was unreliable.

quotes.text: the deceased died of a gun-shot wound which could be ascribed to a .12 bore weapon, not a rifle which was with the accused. Moreover, some of the empty cartridges lifted from the spot did not match with the rifles of the three accused thereby giving rise to a possibility that someone else was also present with a rifle and had used it.
the prosecution failed to prove that those three policemen in uniform, who attacked Raj Kumar Baliyan (the deceased), were the persons facing trial.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that an appellate court must not interfere with an order of acquittal merely because a contrary view is permissible, particularly where the trial court's view is a plausible one based on proper evidence appreciation.

quotes.text: it is equally settled that the appellate court must not interfere with an order of acquittal merely because a contrary view is permissible, particularly, where the view taken by the trial court is a plausible view based on proper appreciation of evidence and is not vitiated by ignorance/misreading of relevant evidence on record.
